claims.text: An engineered ultrafine near-surface microstructure gives high-entropy alloys superior resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion relative to a coarse-grained surface.
Refining the near-surface microstructure to ultrafine or ultra-nanocrystalline grain sizes increases near-surface grain-boundary density.
Increased grain-boundary density accelerates dynamic repassivation after mechanical removal of a passive film.
Grain boundaries are preferential reactive sites for rapid formation of a passive oxide film.
Rapid repassivation continuously restores the protective film during tribocorrosion.
Continuous restoration of the passive film mitigates both wear and corrosion under combined degradation conditions.
Under identical tribocorrosion conditions, the ultrafine near-surface variant will have a lower friction coefficient than the coarse-grained baseline.
Under identical tribocorrosion conditions, the ultrafine near-surface variant will have a lower wear rate than the coarse-grained baseline.
Under identical tribocorrosion conditions, the ultrafine near-surface variant will exhibit smaller open-circuit-potential shifts than the coarse-grained baseline.
Smaller open-circuit-potential shifts indicate more stable passive-film behavior.
The coarse-grained baseline has fewer grain boundaries than the ultrafine variant.
The coarse-grained baseline repassivates more slowly after wear-induced passive-film removal.
The proposed benefit should occur only when mechanical wear and corrosive attack act simultaneously.
In inert or purely mechanical environments, increased grain-boundary density may not provide the proposed performance benefit.
Prior evidence supports a role for grain-boundary density in dynamic repassivation.
Residual stresses or secondary phases could also contribute to the observed tribocorrosion behavior.
